That in the opinion of this House the experience of the provinces which have taken over the telephone system and the evidence collected by a special committee of this House appointed to inquire into the question of telegrams and telephones more than four years ago, establish the fact that the people of Canada, outside the zone of provincially operated lines, are paying far higher rates for telephone service than they should be called upon to pay.
That i tis the immediate duty of the government to initiate and carry out such measures as will remove long existing abuses in this regard and secure to the people of Canada, ether than the people of Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba, a rate of service at least as moderate as, having regard to local conditions, nrevails countries where a national telephone service is maintained.
He said: Mr. Speaker: This is a business proposition, and I propose, in my activities in this House, to limit myself as far as possible to business propositions, and to endeavour to bring about, as far as I can, better conditions for the people generally. The question of an amelioration of our condition as regards telephone service is, comparatively speaking, new. It did not occur to our people perhaps as early as it did to the peonle of the United States, that we were not enjoving as good conditions in this respect as we were entitled to. Even in the United States, down to the year 1894. the Bell Telephone Company had practically a monopoly of the service in that country, and it was only about that time that the people began to awake to the fact, that thev could do better than to allow this monopolv 56
to continue. It was considerably later than that before it began to dawn upon us that we also were entitled to a better condition of things. Perhaps it was not until about the beginning of this century that we began to realize that we were paying too much, and not getting as good a service as we were entitled to; and from that time onward the feeling has been gradually growing stronger in Canada that we should do something to rid ourselves of the monopoly of the Bell Telephone Co. But, although there was a good leal of agitation on the subject in the House, no definite action was taken until 1904, when Sir Wm. Mulock moved the resolution which resulted in a special committee being appointed to investigate the matter. This government was certainly not more alert than it ought to have been in appointing that committee. Now, I w.ould suppose that that committee was appointed for some business object, and that object, as I understand, was to ascertain whether or not we could put ourselves in a better position; and if the result of that investigation was to show that the conditions were not satisfactory, some action would be taken. From that time down to the present no action has been taken; nothing has been done to relieve the people of Canada from the conditions under which they were suffering. There are many men in this House far more familiar with telephonic conditions than I am, and better able to stir up the government to get a move on in this matter, but in the absence of anybody else taking it up, I took it upon myself at. the beginning of this session to place this resolution on the Order Paper with a view of righting the wrongs which the investigation of the committee of 1904 showed to exist in the Dominion of Canada.
Now my resolution aims at two things. My first proposition is that we are paying too much for our telephone service, and I may add that our telephone service is not as complete or as good as it ought to be. My second proposition is that we are entitled to have as cheap a service as those countries where national telephones have been established. The members of this House are very familiar with these propositions. When we talk of nationalizing our railways or any of our public utilities, the answer from the honourable gentlemen opposite is this-and I have heard it from the right honourable the leader of the government down-that we can get a cheaper service and a more efficient service from a company service. Now. we have a company service, and according to the decision of the government we are to continue _ to have a company service, and that being the case, it is for us to see to it. as far as possible, that a company, being able to give a cheaper service than a government can, shall give us at least as cheap a service as

is enjoyed in countries where a government service is given. At the time the investigation took place, the committee took evidence from various important bodies as to what they thought was the best system for Canada. There were two classes of advocates: One was for the ownership by the government of the entire telephonic system in Canada, the other was for the ownership by the government of the trunk lines only, with the branch lines and local services in the hands of companies or other parties. Among those who advocated complete government ownership were the Toronto city council, the Owen Sound board of trade, the county council of Bruce, the city of Nanaimo, the town of Simcoe, the township of Pickering, the town of Port Perry, the Regina board of trade, the Montreal chambers of commerce, the Stratford board of trade, the town of Morris, Man., the municipality of Pipestone, Man., the municipality of Batisean, Que., the municipality of Matsqui, B.C., the municipality of Jordan, B.C., the municipality of Maple Creek, N.W.T., the municipality of Rama, the county of Essex, the town of Hespeler and the councils of the towns and county, the trades and labour councils and the boards of trade of the county of Waterloo.
Among those who advocated government ownership of long distance lines, were Kelowna in British Columbia; the Ontario Municipal Association; the Union of Canadian Municipalities, which is an important body representing the matured thought of the entire municipal bodies of Canada, which I think is not an unimportant element in the discussion of any public question in Canada. There was the town of Peterborough; the Winnipeg Printers' board of trade; the retail merchants of Ontario, 5,000 strong; the Guelph board of trade; town of Orangeville; town of Neepa-wa; town of St. Andrew's, New Brunswick; Union Telephone Company, Florenceville, New Brunswick; municipality of Gormley, Ontario, county of Elgin; township of York; town of Weston; Halifax county, Nova Scotia; town of Sarnia. I have said that the government pronouncing judgment in this House and repeating it everywhere, that we can have a better and more efficient service by leaving it in the hands of companies than we can by having it operated under government authority, directly by the action of a minister or indirectly through the action of a commission, it is up to the government, if I may use that expression, to see to it now that we have at least as cheap a service, as efficient a service. as they have in those countries where nationalization has been established. Now, the House will remember that in the course of that investigation we employed an eminent expert, a Mr. Dagger, who was expected to collect material and boil it down, as it were, to crystallize it and to present it to the committee. That being the case, I Mr. LENNOX.

I have been trying to go with them hand in hand, as it were, and I hope I shall be able to do them a great deal of good. This measure which I advocate in my resolution is one which affects almost every person in Canada. Take a telephone rate of four cents for fifteen miles in Australia and of 4$ cents in some countries for 120 miles, and you can see that if we can get telephone rates on anything like the reasonable basis in effect in these countries where they have nationalized their system, we will be extending a great boon to the people of our rural districts. It is the rural districts in which I am most concerned. I feel that what is driving the young man away from the farm is that he has not the modern conveniences and advantages which are possessed by his relatives in the cities, and if you want to get the young man back to the land you have to make rural life more comfortable. I hope that when we conserve our water-powers and by their means carry the electric light into every barn and the dwelling of every farm in Canada, and when we bring the telephone and the telegraph at reasonable rates to every farm home, and when our postal facilities give a daily mail service to almost all parts of the country, then will our young men be encouraged to live upon the farm, and then will a great step be taken for the betterment of Canada.

The closing words of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lennox) remind us that when the millennium comes we will be a happy people living in a happy world. We are told by the hon. gentleman that his resolution is moved in a spirit friendly to the administration, and I will allow that statement of his to pass without comment, further than to say that if it was intended to be friendly its language is certainly deceptive. The first part of the resolution contains the premises upon which the hon. gentleman bases his conclusion, and a portion of it reads:

That in the opinion of this House the experience of the provinces which have taken over the telephone system establish the fact that the people of Canada, outside the zone of provincially operated lines, are paying for higher rates for telephone service than they should he called upon to pay.
The language employed there is certainly not very clear, but I assume the hon. gentleman intended these words to mean, that in the three prairie provinces in which they have assumed the ownership and control of the telephone system, there has followed a reduction in rates, which causes the existing rates to be lower than the rates in other provinces. If there is any efficacy in an argument based on that portion of the resolution, the hon. gentleman must have failed in his proof because the telephone rates in the three prairie provinces are not lower than they are in any of the other provinces of Canada. The resolution was placed upon the Order Paper on January the 21st last, and it is hardly fair for the hon. gentleman to claim that by reason of its publicity at that date he forced the government of Manitoba to make some slight reductions recently. The conclusion of the resolution is based upon another statement of fact, which, as is the case of the former portion of the resolution, is not correct. It says:
"That the evidence collected by a special committee of this House appointed to enquire into the question of telegraphs and telephones more than four years ago, established the fact that the people of Canada, outside the zone of provincially operated lines, are paying far higher rates for telephone service than they should be called upon to pay.'
Now, Mr. Speaker, I assume that when the hon. gentleman undertakes to state that in any one province of Canada we are paying higher telephone rates than we should, he means that the private or company owned and operated telephone lines are earning more than a reasonable profit. Once in a while, a province does become the proprietor of the telephone system and engages in its operations. I fear, however, that the motive prompting provincial governments to engage in this work is not so much commercial as political. I think that is fairly true of Manitoba. In a series of letters addressed to the London ' Times,' he promised that, if the post office would give his company a license to operate a telephone system, he would give to the five millions of people in the London metropolitan district a metallic circuit service at $50 or $60 a year, very much less than the rates charged by the Post Office, or by the National Telephone Company, the chief telephone company of England. He had an experience of one year and found that he could not give the telephone service at anything like the rate he had led the people to expect. He sold out his plant to the National Telephone Company, and, later, he admitted, in a letter to the ' Times ' that in talking about $50 and $60 telephone rates he certainly had ' done a great deal of bleating.' And I think that Messrs. Rogers, Roblin and Campbell, of Manitoba, have ' done a great deal of bleating ' in promising the telephone reductions they have promised to the public. They make very little allowance for depreciation in the telephone plant. This of course varies, different telephone companies employ different methods of calculating depreciation. Some assign values for depreciation of the plant divided up into ten or twelve portions, the wires are given a certain period of life and the poles a certain period; some telephone companies write off ten per cent and some five per cent, but I think that in most cases eight per cent would be considered a very fair amount to write off for depreciation. The government of Manitoba spent $104,000 for

maintenance of their telephone system in 1908, and they did not write off anything in addition for depreciation. The question of telephones in Manitoba was inquired into before a special committee of the legislature of that province in 1906. The Hon. I challenge any person to controvert that in the slightest degree whatever, and I repeat W'hat I have already said, that the result is not favourable to the administration and that the telephone system in 1908 in Manitoba was operated at a loss. I deny that my hon. friend who moves this resolution

can obtain anything from the experience of the province of Manitoba to justify the conclusions which he asks this House to affirm. Then, there is this to be remembered t The government of Manitoba have been in charge of the operation of this system for but one year, and I think it is fair to say that they have not yet had that experience which would warrant them in embarking upon the policy of rate reduction. I submit that the people of Manitoba would have justified the government in abstaining from any reduction of these rates for a further period at least. Again, it should be remembered that Manitoba is a growing province, and that it is a peculiar thing that the telephone business is different from almost all other commercial businesses in that as your volume of business increases your profits do not necessarily grow, and there comes a period, in the telephone business when, if you receive a certain number of subscribers, you commence to lose money. In most other businesses the greater the volume the greater the profits. This is rather an important point, and I wish to read what a telephone paper called ' Public Service ' says in answer to a question asked upon this point. This question is often asked concerning the telephone business. Take, for instance, the city of Brandon. It is a young and growing town. The average length of wires in that town to-day is half a mile. This town will grow in all directions and what change will this effect? They will have to increase the length of the wire lines per subscriber, and consequently there will be a greater initial cost per station and a larger maintenance cost. In the second place, the increased number of subscribers increases the number of calls at the central office, and this necessarily increases the labour in connection with the central office. Of course, it also means an increase of rates. Now, I wish to read one of a series of answers given to a question by a correspondent of this paper, the question being: Why are telephone rates higher in a large city than in a small city or town? The writer who answers this question says:
As the number of subscribers increases, the number of calls per station increases correspondingly, and, as an operator can only handle a certain number of calls per hour, extra operators are required. This item of expense in a large exchange, as compared to the same item of expense in a small exchange, is very large. By way of illustration, and to account for the increase in the number of calls per station with the increase in the number of stations, it can readily be seen that in an exchange of 1,000 stations a subscriber can only call 999 other subscribers, whereas a subscriber in an exchange of 10,000 subscribers can call 9,999 other subscribers, and being able to do this it is natural to suppose that the calls per station will be materially increased with the addition of other subscribers.
The above reasons are only a few of the many that can be advanced to show the necessity for charging higher rates in a large city than in a small one. It is now a generally well known fact that the telephone business is altogether unlike any other, for where cost is usually decreased the bulk of business increases in any commercial business, the reverse is true in the operation of a telephone plant. As the number of subscribers increases, the cost of installation and operation increases proportionally, which necessarily compels the charging of higher rates from time to time as subscribers are added to the exchange.
The hon. gentleman in his resolution refers also to the other provinces, of Alberta and Saskatchewan. He does not mention them, it is true, but in general terms he refers to them, as I assume they are included in the prairie .provinces. My hon. friend attempts to draw some conclusions from the experience of these prairie provinces and, as he asks hon. gentlemen to base a judgment favourable to this resolution upon that experience, I beg to say there is nothing in the experience of the province of Saskatchewan to justify anybody in supporting his resolution because in that province they have had no telephone experience as yet. At the last session of the legislature the government of that province took power to instal and operate trunk lines, to empower municipalities to engage in the telephone business and to aid farmers' lines to the extent of giving them free poles. I therefore say that the hon. gentleman can find nothing in the experience of Saskatchewan to sustain his resolution, and consequently his resolution is, at least to the extent of one-third of it, absolutely vitiated. I might at considerable length give the result of telephone operation in the province of Alberta, but I wish to be brief, and I will simply say that there has been no reduction whatever in rates in that province since it took over the Bell Telephone system. Neither the government nor any member of the government has made any promise to the public that the rates would be reduced, and indeed I may say that the telephone rates in Alberta are higher than they are in the county represented by the hon. gentleman.
Does the honourable gentleman say that his friends in Alberta and Saskatchewan were wrong in taking over the telephone system?

If the honourable gentleman wants my own personal opinion,
I will answer that I believe it was a bad policy. I say that the telephone rates in all the western provinces are no lower to-day than they are in any town or city in Ontario of corresponding size. There has been no reduction of rates in Alberta, and on the authority of statements made by the Calgary newspapers and the Calgary

Board of Trade, I say that the province of Alberta is not giving to its subscribers as good a service as was given by the Bell Telephone Company. The honourable gentleman says that Canada is suffering from a telephone monopoly and that we are in an inferior position to other countries with respect to the telephone service, but he also tells us that he offers no argument for or against government ownership. As I have pointed out it is not fair to compare telephone rates in this country with the rates prevailing in France ot in Italy or in Australia. The question is:	Are the private
telephone companies in this country giving as good a service as they possibly can, and are they giving that service at as cheap a rate as they can consistent with maintaining their plant efficiently and allowing themselves an adequate return on the capital employed? I do not think that Canada is prepared at this stage to assume the enormous financial burden of taking over the telephone systems. It would be a serious matter also to add to the Civil Service list of the country the employees of the telephone service. Successive postmasters general and chancellors of the exchequor in Great Britain have given as a reason against the taking over, of the National Telephone Company that it would be a menace to the country to add its employees to the already over burdened civil list. The experience of the British post office is that they cannot get the same efficiency in the unit in the telephone service as the National Telephone Co. gets from its operators. However, assuming for the sake of argument that there is a grievance against the telephone companies, is there not a better remedy than nationalization of the telephones? After the evidence was taken by a select committee of this House some years ago the government no doubt took this matter into consideration and last year the Kailway Act was amended by placing telegraphs and telephones under the control of the Railway Commission. By that Act of last year the Railway Commissioners are given control over the rates of telephone companies within the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada; all telephone tolls are made subject to the approval of the board; tolls may be dealt with in the same manner as standard freight rates; the telephone companies are compelled to file with the board the tariff to be charged from time to time; the railway board can compel the company operating a long distance system to grant connections to any telephone system owned and operated by any company, province or municipality; the board can compel that company under terms to make provision for the use of connections; the board is authorized to apply the provisions of the Railway Act with respect to joint tariffs to the interchange of business Mr. A. K. MACLEAN.
between telephone companies, and all working agreements between telephone companies as to interchange of business are to be approved by the board. Now, the question is, does not this legislation put the telephone companies of this country sufficiently under the control of the Board of Railway Commissioners to ensure to the people due and ample protection as to telephone rates? I submit that it does, and I submit that the policy at present contained in our legislation in this regard is the proper policy. The Railway Commissioners have already taken a great deal of evidence concerning telephone rates in this country, and they should be given ample opportunity to study this question, and no doubt m due course they will make such regulations as to rates as will afford ample protection to the public. The Railway Board has, I think, secured a reputation _ for business which is commendable to itself and is satisfactory to the people of this country generally; and if the telephone companies operating in this country are doing an injustice to their subscribers and to the public generally, as the mover of this resolution suggests, I think we may well hope that ample relief will be accorded by the Railway Commission. I do not wish to delay the House further on this matter; but m closing, I desire, seconded by Mr. Sinclair, to move this amendment:

this statement that comes from the legislature of Manitoba:
The maintenance and. efficiency of the plant, equipment, long distance and farmers' rural lines have been kept up during the year by the expenditure of $98,699.99 for material, travelling expenses and labour.
All the telephone companies, municipal systems and others in the province who are doing business independently of the Bell Company, have been accorded connection with the government system, thereby adding to the value of all telephones which now comprise a system of over 20,000 subscribers. They are the men who are building up companies composed of farmers, and who find it impossible to get the Bell Telephone Company to put in their lines at any reasonable figure. I would like to take you into a township I have in mind at the present time. On the one side the Bell Telephone Company is charging the farmers $20 a year and compelling them to subscribe for three years, and to furnish enough subscribers to build a line several times over before they will begin operations; while on the other side of the township is an independent telephone company with some 200 subscribers, and they only charge $6 per annum, and are able to show a splendid surplus at the end of the year. I have in my possession the annual statement of that independent company and it shows that these men, through good business

management, had been able to develop a spleindid telephone service that covers a great deal of territory and are able to give to the people in those rural districts that service for $6 per annum, and show a surplus at the end of the year.
Now my hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) is simply urging upon the government the necessity of investigating this important question. Four or five years ago we had a great deal of useful information placed before that Telephone Committee, information that has never been given to the public except through the medium of the speeches of my hon, friend for South Simcoe. What we need is a more progressive policy along the line of telephones and telegraphs in this country. From what I was able to gather when I was over in the old land in regard to telephone and telegraph systems, I am satisfied that with proper business management and government control of these public utilities we could make them paying concerns, and at the same time cut the prices in two. The hon. gentleman from Lunenburg (Mr. Maclean) gave us the example of the city of Glasgow; he said the city of Glasgow had turned over the independent telephone company to the Post Office Department. But he had to tell us at the same time that the reason they had a deficit was chiefly owing to the fact that they were fighting the National Telenhone Company in that great city of Glasgow. No other reason can be brought forward to show that if they had exhibited reasonably fair business abilities, they would have had a surplus at the end of the year.

The city of Glasgow had a tremendous advantage over the National Telephone Company, because the corporation of Glasgow would not allow the National Company to put its wires under ground. They were obliged in many cases to string their wires from housetop to housetop. It was sheer inability on the part of the municipality successfully to operate a telephone company.

At the same time the government turns round and buys it out, and to-day what do we find in regard to the management of telephones in Great Britain? It was my privilege only last year to show to the Prime Minister, answering a statement of his in regard to telephones and telegraphs in Great Britain that I do not think he would attempt to repeat to-night, that instead of the companies not being paying investments there, they are paying investments, and they are giving a most satisfactory service to the people of that country. I agree with my hon. friend from Lunenburg that a few years ago the telephone system of Great Britain was anything but satisfactory, and we would not like to see in the Dominion of Canada the system they Mr. ARMSTRONG.
had there at that time. But I want to tell my hon. friend that that system has been wonderfully improved, and that to-day it is getting to be almost as perfect a system as you can find anywhere.

I would like to remind my hon. friend of this fact also, that Great Britain is only in the telephone business to preserve her telegraph business. They know they will always lose money by the telephones.

I have listened with great interest to the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox), in fact I always listen to him with much interest, because he prepares his speeches well and is usually fair in his presentation of his facts. I have listened also to the somewhat impassioned appeal of the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) on behalf of the farmers. I think many of those on this side, as well as those opposite, can join in that very laudable aim. In so far as these hon. gentlemen are asking the government to take steps to make sure that the people of this country get their telephone services as cheaply as possible, I am heartily in accord with them, as also, I am sure, is every hon. member on this side. I am hardly at one, however, with my hon. friend from South Simcoe in his interpretation of the meaning of the first part of the resolution he has moved. As I understand this resolution, it asks this House to declare that the result of the operation of telephones in those provinces of Canada in which they have been controlled by the government is that the people receive their telephones cheaper than do the people of those provinces in which the telephones are not controlled by the government. If that be the case, I must say that I do not agree with him. I can speak very intelligently so far as one province is concerned, and I think I can speak with some intelligence so far as another province, the province of Manitoba, is concerned. I am not going to follow my hon. friends in their statements concerning telephonic affairs on the continent of Europe.



I have not been there to examine into the subject, and, so far as I know, neither have the hon. gentlemen who have spoken. I read the evidence taken before the Telephone Committee with a great deal of interest, and have listened with interest to the quotation of it by these hon. gentlemen. But I would point out that that evidence was given four years ago, and that in the four years that have elapsed there have been a great many changes in the telephone business. The hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. A. K. Maclean) referred to the fact that Glasgow, one of the cities put forward as a model from a municipal standpoint, has gone out of the telephone business because it could not make the business pay. And I would point out that, notwithstanding that there has been a very serious agitation for better control of telephones all over Canada and the United States in the last four years, in nearly every part of Canada and the United States telephone rates have increased rather than decreased. As has been pointed out by the hon. member for Lunenburg, the more the telephone business increases the greater in proportion will be the increase in the cost. It is different from other public utilities or other businesses. In my own town four years ago we were getting business telephones for $10 and residence telephones for $5, and those long distance telephones at that. Five years ago we were able to talk from Woodstock to St. John, 140 miles, for 25 cents. To-day we pay 55 cents. All over Canada you will find the rates have been increased. In any province of Canada, so far as I know, five years ago the long distance rate was based on a five minute conversation; to-day it is based on a three-minute conversation in every province except Manitoba, where it is two minutes. I point this out only to show that, notwithstanding the agitation that has been carried on in the country, telephone rates have been going up and the municipalities have not been taking control of this public utility or going into the telephone business. The only province in Canada which has gone into the telephone business with anything like thoroughness has been Manitoba.
It is not my purpose to deal with telephone matters in European countries. I need not point out that the conditions in Europe are very different from those in Canada. In the first place we know that wages are much higher here than in continental Europe, that you can operate a telephone system, so far as wages are concerned, in most European countries for fifty per cent of what you have to pay in Canada. I can apply almost the same percentage to Great Britain.
Would that apply to Australia?

No, I do not think so.
I want to be fair and I think that in all the arguments put forward by the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) to-night the Australian proposition looks to be the cheapest telephone communication we have discussed. But I want also to point out that my hon. friend did not state the capital involved in Australia, whether or not there was a deficit or anything with regard to the maintenance of the telephone system there, for instance the amount set aside for depreciation.
If I recollect I read out what the service was in Australia.

Then I did not catch it, but if the hon. gentleman did give that information I stand corrected. My purpose is to discuss this subject from a Canadian standpoint. It is not to my mind a question of what they have done in England, in France, in Bavaria, in Sweden or in Norway. Conditions are different in these countries from what they are here. The important question is what have we done in Canada up to the present and what can we do in the future? I again assure my hon. friends that although I am somewhat interested in the telephone business in one province, I am as anxious as my hon. friends to see the people of Canada get telephone communication at a proper rate. My hon. friend from Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) spent some time discussing the iniquities of the Bell Telephone Company. I hold no brief for the Bell Telephone Company. I am willing to admit that in many cases all over Canada the Bell Telephone Company have been monopolists and I dare say they have many sins to answer for. I am not trying to excuse or exculpate or even to apologize for them, but I wish to discuss for a few moments the actual conditions of the telephone business as they exist in Canada to-day. It has been said here to-night, and I presume will be again by my hon. friends on the other side of the House, that the experience of the province of Manitoba in the last year has justified the statement made so many times by hon. gentlemen opposite in the last three or four years, that all public utilities should be owned, operated and controlled by governments and municipalities, and not by corporations; or in other words the doctrine of public ownership.
Oh, no.

I am glad my hon. friend says 'oh, no,' because the only logical conclusion of the argument we have heard to-night is that the government should take control of these utilities and operate them themselves.

No one on this side has made any suggestion, and I distinctly said I was not arguing the question of public

ownership pro or con. I was saying we should have as cheap a service in Canada as having relation to the conditions existing in other countries where they have a national system would be possible.

The hon. gentleman has correctly repeated what he said earlier in the evening, but I again repeat that the logical conclusion of his argument is that we must have public ownership because the only instances he has given where they have cheaper telephones than in Canada are in those countries where government ownership is in existence and telephones are owned and controlled by the government.
In Manitoba the government have been operating their telephone system for a year and as was pointed out by my hon. friend they had a surplus in that year of something like $380,000. I think lie was wrong in that, that he was including in it $161,00 ) which should have been paid for interest.

neous. Therefore we have $238,132. I know that the custom prevails in Manitoba and I know that at any time the Manitoba government have in their hands not less than $100,000 in money which they have not earned or paid for. I find from an analysis of the statement issued by the Minister of Public Works for the province of Manitoba, about the 22nd or 23rd of February, that last year they received from rentals-and that means what we, as subscribers all over the country will pay for having a telephone in our house-at least $535,465. one quarter, or $100,000, of this amount paid in advance every three months. At no time in the year would they have less than $100,000 in their possession, representing rentals that had not been earned. But, if in January, 1908, they had $108,000 in their hands, it is only fair to assume, if they obtained 2,000 additional subscribers, that they should have $120,000 in their hands at the end of the year, and therefore I am going to assume, when they made up this statement and when Mr. Bogers made this statement in the legislature of Manitoba that thev had in their possession $120,000 which they had not earned. Any person must admit that that should be deducted from the gross revenue of the province for that year.
Now, that brings us to another question and that is the question of depreciation. I do not have to argue to any hon. gentleman in this house nor to any gentleman in the country, farmer, or merchant, or telephone manager that there will be a depreciation every year in a telephone line. I can tell you what the experience of the New Brunswick Telephone Company has shown that our poles, which are always 25 feet long by 6 inches at the top, have to be renewed every twelve or fifteen years on the average, and that cross arms which cost about forty *or forty-five cents each have to be renewed every seven or eight years on the average. That is what is called depreciation. I can point out to you more than that. There is not a telephone company in Canada that has not, in the last twenty-five years, been compelled, practically to discard every switchboard in its service. They have been compelled to discard the Blake transmitter and the short distance transmitter by the thousands and tens of thousands all over Canada. Go to the Bell Telephone Company, the Nova Scotia Telephone Company, the New Brunswick Telephone Company, or any big telephone company in Canada or the United States and they will show you whole warehouses almost filled with discarded telephone instruments. They have been compelled to put in long distance equipment and in less than ten years they will be compelled to discard the present apparatus and put in some other arrangement. These are some of the incidents that, go towards depreciation in plant which must be provided for by any well regulated telephone company. There are various items which go to make up the amount that should be set aside to provide for depreciation. The New Brunswick Telephone Company consider that they must set aside eight per cent of the total cost of the investment in order to provide depreciation. Some companies go as high as ten per cent and some companies as low as five per cent, but in no company is it possible to get along with an expenditure of less than five per cent for depreciation-not Mr. CARVELL.
maintenance. My hon. friend from Lamb-ton (Mr. Armstrong) will pardon me if I tell him that he is a little mixed as to the meaning of these terms. The word ' maintenance ' means ordinary little expenses that have to be incurred every day in the week and every month in the year in keeping your line in fairly good working order. It means that if a cross arm breaks you must put it up again, it means that if an insulator breaks, as thousands and thousands do in the year, it must be repaired, it means that if you have a sleetstorm, such as we had a month ago by which tens of thousands of dollars worth of wires and poles are broken down to the ground, they must be repaired. All of these things are incidents in the operation of every telephone company which must be provided for every day and every week and these are the incidents which go to make up the maintenance. When we speak of five per cent tor depreciation we do not mean this at all. We refer to a sum of money not less than five per cent on the cost of the investment which is actually necessary to renlace a pole that becomes rotten, to replace a cross arm when it becomes rotten, to replace a switchboard when it becomes obsolete, or in other words to keep the whole telephone system in such a condition that it will be a well working concern. If you add to the statement of the Manitoba government the sum of five per cent for depreciation you make an addition there of $165,000. There is no telephone man on earth who will say that you can keep the Manitoba telephone system up to a proper state of repair, system costing $3,300,000. for less than $165,000 per annum and if you add these sums together you have a total of $446,000 and your total balance, after subtracting expenditures from receipts will be only $380,000; or, in other words, if these figures be correct the operation by the Manitoba government of the telephones lines for eleven and a half months, instead of showing a surplus of $232,000, shows a deficit of $55,998.
I am prepared to meet any actuary or any practical telephone man whom the province of Manitoba may appoint and go over these figures with them, and I am satisfied they will not differ with me to the extent of $10,000. I have stated that no telephone company would for a moment hope to get along by expending for maintenance and depreciaion a less amount than for operation, and if you take the operation at $238,000, and the depreciation and maintenance at a like amount, and the unearned rentals at $120,000, and the interest at $161,000 and add these together you have $757,264 as against a total revenue of only 722,612, or a deficit of $34,632. I therefore repeat that instead of having a surplus of $232,000, by any mode of intelligent figuring which they possibly can devise there

must be a deficit of anywhere between $25,000 and $50,000 in the operation of the telephones in Manitoba last year. I state here to-night, and I think I can prove it to the satisfaction of the House, that the proposed reduction foreshadowed by the Minister of Public Works in Winnipeg on Thursday night are in reality no reductions at all. The hon. gentleman from Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) read a statement to the effect that they had reduced the joint user telephone from $25 to $15. But, does the hon. gentleman realize what joint user in telephone means. I doubt if there is a gentleman in this chamber who ever knew of the joint user of a telephone. I do not know of one in my own town; if there are any in New Brunswick they are very few, and I venture to say that there are not one hundred joint users in the whole city of Winnipeg. Joint user of a telephone means that once in a while in a big city you will find, say a collecting lawyer and an insurance agent occupying adjoining rooms as offices and they both pay a certain amount for the telephone they use in common. I doubt if you will find one hundred such in Winnipeg, and yet this is one of the lemons that the Manitoba government throw out to the people and say look what we are doing for you. And, as the joint user in residences; where will you find two families using the same phone.
You will find hundreds, perhans thousands of instances in Toronto where families occupying flats use one telephone and contribute jointly to the rental.
That would be in an hotel.
No.
That would be what we call P.B.X., or private branch exchange.
We get a telephone in Toronto for $50 and all the people in that house use it.
Meanwhile the telephone company is getting $5 for the telephone.
You can tell the company that two families will use the telephone in a private house and instead of charging $30 each they charge $50 and there are hundreds of cases of that kind.
That is so, but does the hon. gentleman mean to say that the government of Manitoba will allow two families to have a telephone in their house and charge them only $10.
My opinion is that the government of Manitoba will allow two families the joint use of a telephone in a private residence for $10.
That is what you mean?
That is what I understand.

Then I simply say I
don't believe it.
And the last announcement of the Postmaster General in England provides for the same kind of joint user.

We are discussing Manitoba, not England, and I do not believe the government of Manitoba will give two families the right to use a telephone for $10, when they will charge one family $24. If my hon. friend can find any comfort in a reduction of that kind he can have it, but there is a great big nigger in the wood pile somewhere in this proposed reduction of the Manitoba telephone rates.
There is a reduction from $24 to $18.

I am willing to admit that there is a genuine reduction of from 15 per cent to 25 per cent in the residential telephones according to the statement of Mr. Rogers, but outside this residential reduction and the farmers' lines there is practically no reduction at all. This talk about joint user is only a delusion and a snare because people do not go in for joint user. This two party reduction is another delusion and a snare because business men will not use a two party line. A farmer will use a two party or a four party or an eight party line because he cannot help it, but fancy a banker or a lawyer or a doctor or a professional man of any kind using a telephone with another man on the same line; for a two party line means that one can listen to what the other may be saying. In the city of Winnipeg or in the city of Montreal or in any large city there are no two party lines to any extent. I have asked from my friends here about the conditions in Winnipeg and so far as I can learn there are no two party lines in that city. I may be wrong about that, but that is the informaiton I have obtained.
What about the reduction of rates in the towns?

As I understand it the
rate is reduced to *39, and I can tell my hon. friend that in the city of St. John and in the city of Halifax we get a single line for $45, and in the city of Ottawa which is probably as important as the city of Winnipeg, you get a business telephone for $45.
What about the extensions; is there not a reduction there?

Once in a while you will find a man who has a telephone in his hall or his library and he wants another in his bedroom, and he has an extension set put in and that means another

telephone on the same line which will ring at the same time as the main telephone, but the reduction on the extension sets is another delusion and a snare. I do not suppose there are more than two or three gentlemen in this chamber who have in their residences extension sets.
All the government people have them.

I do not think so. I know something about the telephone business, and I can say that not one per cent of the telephones in this country are extension sets; so that when the government of Manitoba tells the people that it is reducing the extension rates from $12 to $6 they are merely deluding them. They charge for business telephones $25 and 2 cents per outcall. Let us see what that means. I do not suppose that any man who uses a telephone in his business makes less than five calls a day; that is 10 cents a day or $30 a year. Now I want to speak for a few minutes on the question of the long distance telephones. My hon. friends opposite when dilating upon the virtues of the Manitoba government and the virtues of public ownership as exemplified by the operations of the Manitoba government, took good care not to refer to the question of tolls. I am going to refer to that for a few minutes, and I make the statement here that the Manitoba government to-day are charging the same tolls which they charged last year, and which the Bell Telephone Company charged, and they are charging ten per cent to 15 per cent more than they are charging in any other portion of Canada for the same service. Let me give a few instances showing a comDarison between Manitoba and New Brunswick-I take New Brunswick because I am best acquainted with that province. I will admit that the service under ten miles is similar in both provinces, 10 cents. When you go above that, beyond 10 miles, there is not a solitary rate in the province of Manitoba but is at least 10 per cent higher than in the province of New Brunswick, or anywhere else in eastern Canada. Now take a few illustrations. In Manitoba, over 10 miles and not exceeding 15 miles, the rate is 15 cents. In New Brunswick I will give a concrete example, namely from St. John to Westfield, a distance of 14 miles, where the rate is only 10 cents. I have here a statement which I will let my hon. friends examine if they care to, showing the rates from the city of St. John to Woodstock and a hundred other points in the province of New Brunswick, and they can figure the distance for themselves. Moreover, the distances in New Brunswick are air lines, and not lines which follow the roads. I do not know whether they figure air lines in Manitoba or not. Now from 20 miles to 35 miles, in Manitoba the rate is 25 cents; while from St. John to Hampton, 22 miles, the

rate is 20 cents. From 45 to 55 miles, the rate in Manitoba is 35 cents, while from St. John to Apohaqui 39 miles the rate is 25 cents. From 85 miles to 130 miles, in Manitoba the rate is 50 cents, while from St. John to Moncton 90 miles the rate is 45 cents. From 130 to 160 miles, in Manitoba, 60 cents; from St .John to Woodstock, 140 miles, 55 cents. From 185 to 200 miles, in Manitoba, 80 cents, from St. John to Andover, 190 miles, 70 cents. From 260 miles to 285 miles, in Manitoba the rate is $1.10; while from St. John to Camp-bellton, 276 miles, it is $1. Those Manitoba rates are all for a 2 minute conversation, ours are for a 3 minute conversation. And yet our friends opposite hold up the results of government ownership in Manitoba as a sample which we should follow in the other provinces of Canada. God forbid that we should ever follow the pace set by the Conservative government in Manitoba in respect to a telephone service.
What is the rate for a 5 minute conversation on the Dominion government owned system, for about 50 to 100 miles?

That is a very intelligent question and requires an equally intelligent answer. I may surprise my hon. friend to tell him that the Dominion government does not own a telephone line, that I know anything about .
I may inform my hon. friend that the Dominion government he supports is operating and owning a telephone system.

Now that I think of it, there are two, I think, in Canada operated by the government. I am told there is one somewhere on the Pacific coast going toward the Yukon, and another away down the St. Lawrence river, somewhere on the Labrador coast.

Allow me to correct the hon. gentleman. Allow me to inform him that there is a system owned and operated by the_ Dominion government extending a good distance down the riding of Yale-Cari-boo. My hon. friend (Mr. Burrell) will have a chance, so far as I know, to give all the information he wishes to. But, to be fair, I would say that the Dominion government is not in the telephone business to such an extent that we can even discuss it at all. What is the use of men talking nonsense and bringing in little quibbles, when we want to deal with facts? I know the Dominion government Mr. CARVELL.

.f-'ARVELL. No, and I don't care. I am talking telephones, not quibbles. There are a number of questions I wish to dis cuss before I leave this important matter. I stated earlier in my remarks that I would attempt to prove that so far as Manitoba is concerned, they have not shown a surplus but a deficit, and have not reduced the rates; and I am willing to leave it to the judgment of this House whether or not I have substantiated my statement. I think I have substantiated it, and I think my hon. friends opposite will get but cold comfort from the consideration of the report presented by the government of Manitoba after their first year's experience in the operation of the telephone. My hon. friend from South Simeoe referred to the remedy, and stated that, in many instances, independent telephone lines have come in and have been able very materially to reduce rates. I admit that four or five years ago, and even as long as ten years ago, there was a great boom of independent telephone lines all over Canada and the United States. And there is no reason why they should not exist to-day. In my own constituency, we have three independent telephone lines, all doing a splendid business. My hon. friend from Lambton thought it a most remarkable thing that an independent telephone line could exist giving a telephone service at six dollars. In my constituency, hundreds of farmers' telephones cost only seven dollars, eight dollars or nine dollars. But, alongside of these, the New Brunswick Telephone Company are getting fifteen dollars for farmers' lines. If hon. gentlemen will take even a few moments to consider it, they will see that a farmers' line can be run at a very cheap rate. But you have perhaps twenty or even thirty subscribers on a line, and a cheap iron wire at that-[DOT]
And fastened to a picket.

Yes, to anything. But it is an accommodation to the people, and while I have some interest in the New Brunswick Telephone Company, I have encouraged the incorporation of farmers' lines as far as I could. In less than three years,
I have had a hand in incorporating two of them. They are a good thing. The farmers are able to have their social gossip. But the man who tries to do business over the line must allow for the fact that every one else knows what he is talking about. And there cannot be a social function any where in the country but every one knows about it. The farmers can get the state of the market, can learn what hogs, potatoes, or oats are worth, the line is a good thing for them. But, when you come to talk about telephone business, the comparison is not at all a fair one. For, in order to have a telephone business, you must have exchanges, you must have long distance connection and every thing else that makes a telephone service. I suppose there is not a switchboard on any farmers' line in Canada that costs $100. But the central switchboard in a town of 4,000 or 5,000 people will cost from $5,000 to $10,000. So, when the hon. gentleman talks about farmers' lines at five dollars or six dollars a year, his discussion is not germane to the subject. There is a big question staring us in the face-are we in Canada paying too much for our telephone service? I must say that the evidence furnished by the government of Manitoba does not prove that the government telephone service is an ideal condition of affairs. How are we to get the rates reduced ? My hon. friend from South Simcoe says by independent companies. I say, all honour to the independent companies. I like to see them go ahead and do all they can. But, I must say, the result of the experience of the independent companies has been anything but favourable from a financial standpoint. I have in mind the case of an independent company started in Portland, Maine, six or seven years ago. They put in what is called the automatic system. Under this system, no central is required; by the manipulation of a portion of the instrument you make your own connection and your own call. At first the company gave ridiculously low rates Afterwards they increased their rates to almost what the old line was charging, but, at the end of five years, they went into a receiver's hands and the shareholders lost about half a million dollars. We find another illustration in Red Deer, Alberta. The Bell Company were charging thirty dollars for business telephones and twenty dollars for residence telephones. A gentleman named
Morte came along from the United States, and claimed that he could give them telephones at about half of what they were paying. The municipality gave a franchise and made a contract, and the system was installed. The rates charged were so low that the Bell Telephone Company got out and left the place entirely to the municipal system-municipal in effect because it was run under municipal control. They started in to give a service at twenty-five dollars for business telephones and ten dollars for residence. After running for a year or two, they found they could not possibly carry on the business at these figures, and gave notice to the municipality under their contract that they would apply for arbitration to fix the rates. The arbitrators, I should judge, were men who would be competent to deal with the matter. One was Mr. Roland Winters, of Lethbridge, the second Mr. R. S. Iielsch, the well known electrical engineer, of Montreal, and the third William Cousins, the mayor of Medicine Hat. After hearing the evidence and taking every thing into consideration, the arbitrators gave their award, which allowed the company to fix its rates at twenty-three dollars for residence telephones and thirty-five dollars for business telephones -about ten or fifteen per cent more than the Bell Company had been charging before the independent company went there at all. Now, let me give a few figures illustrating what independent companies have done in the United States. I state that not an independent company has been doing a telephone business-I differentiate between a telephone business and a farmers' line-for ten years, or even five years, that has not been compelled to increase its rates :

1 rise to oppose the adjournment of the debate except on some

reasonable terms. We have sat here hour after hour listening to hon. gentlemen opposite speaking well, speaking eloquently I admit, but not speaking to the question we should be discussing, not speaking to the question I brought forward. The government have a duty to perform in this matter, but they have not made any statement as to what course they intend to pursue. The country will expect us to debate this matter and dispose of it in some reasonable way. I ask the right hon. gentleman who leads the House (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) if he will say that he will give an opportunity of continuing this debate. In that event I have no objection to its being adjourned; otherwise, I must insist that we should either dispose of it by vote now, or decide upon the question of adjournment as the rules of the House provide.

In the few words just uttered by my hon. friend (Mr. Lennox) there are many things to which I could take exception. He said the question has not been debated on this side. In my humble opinion it has been well debated. In so far as the government are concerned, I may say we are disposed to accept the amendment moved by the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. A. K. Maclean). I will not undertake at this period of the session to say whether it will come up again; perhaps it will, perhaps it will not. My hon. friend (Mr. Lennox) has had at least six or seven different opportunities of bringing up this question before to-day.
